jsonld.name: Full English Breakfast Hash
jsonld.description: The full English collapsed into one pan and one dish: potatoes, bacon, sausage, black pudding, mushroom, and tomato all diced and fried together into a browned, layered hash, with eggs cracked over the top and baked in place until the whites set and the yolks stay running. It is the full English's architecture with the assembly step deleted — everything cooks in one pan, the fat economy runs itself, and the eggs baste in the accumulated essence of the entire breakfast. The hash is a genuinely old breakfast form — the café's "mixed grill hash" and the American skillet's British cousin — and it is the most forgiving way to feed four people a full English from a single frying pan. The discipline is dicing: everything cut to a size that cooks in the same window, and the patience to build the potato crust undisturbed before the stirring begins.

skeleton:
Full English Breakfast Hash

British · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The full English collapsed into one pan and one dish: potatoes, bacon, sausage, black pudding, mushroom, and tomato all diced and fried together into a browned, layered hash, with eggs cracked over the top and baked in place until the whites set and the yolks stay running. It is the full English's architecture with the assembly step deleted — everything cooks in one pan, the fat economy runs itself, and the eggs baste in the accumulated essence of the entire breakfast. The hash is a genuinely old breakfast form — the café's "mixed grill hash" and the American skillet's British cousin — and it is the most forgiving way to feed four people a full English from a single frying pan. The discipline is dicing: everything cut to a size that cooks in the same window, and the patience to build the potato crust undisturbed before the stirring begins.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The hash base

  • no need to par-boil; raw dice roasts beautifully in the pan's fat

The eggs and finish

- **Uniform 1.5 cm dice is the recipe's spine.** Everything — potato, black pudding, mushroom — at the same size means one cooking window and even browning. This is fifteen minutes of knife work that makes the pan behave. - **A wide, heavy pan with a lid** — 28–30 cm, cast iron ideal. The lid does two jobs: it steams the raw potato dice through in the first stage, and it sets the egg whites at the end. - **The eggs at room temperature** so the whites set in the same time the pan needs to reheat.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • Potatoes: golden two-face crust, fluffy centre, crust preserved through later stages.
  • Meats: browned sequentially in the pan's centre, fond deglazed into the hash.
  • Eggs: whites steam-set, yolks liquid; checked by straight lid-lift.
  • The pan's bottom layer: the deepest crust, served with ceremony.

Full English Breakfast Hash

Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 35 minutes · Total: 50 minutes · Serves 4

Ingredients

The hash base

  • 800 g floury potatoes (Maris Piper), cut into 1.5 cm dice — no need to par-boil; raw dice roasts beautifully in the pan's fat
  • 4 rashers (200 g) smoked back bacon, diced small
  • 4 pork sausages (320 g), skins removed, meat broken into nuggets
  • 150 g black pudding, cut into 1.5 cm dice
  • 200 g chestnut mushrooms, quartered
  • 1 medium onion (150 g), diced
  • 2 tomatoes (240 g), deseeded and diced

The eggs and finish

  • 4 large eggs (220 g)
  • 30 g butter
  • 15 ml / 14 g neutral oil
  • 3 g fine sea salt
  • 1 g black pepper
  • 2 g fresh thyme leaves, or ½ tsp dried
  • 10 ml mushroom ketchup (optional, stirred in at the end)
  • Brown breakfast sauce and toast, to serve

Instructions

  1. **Steam-fry the potatoes — 12 minutes covered.** Heat the oil in the pan over medium heat, add the potato dice with half the salt, toss to coat, then add 60 ml of water, cover, and cook 10 minutes, until the water has evaporated and the dice are nearly tender. Uncover, add 15 g of the butter, raise the heat to medium-high, and fry 4–5 minutes, turning only twice, until two faces of most dice are golden. Checkpoint — the potato dice are golden-crusted on their faces, fluffy within, and the pan's base carries a lace of fond. The crust has been built; the next stages must preserve it.
  2. **Brown the meats in the pan — 8 minutes.** Push the potatoes to the pan's edges and add the sausage nuggets to the centre. Cook 3 minutes to brown, then add the bacon dice for 3 minutes more, then the black pudding dice for a final 2 minutes, folding everything together at the end. Deglaze the fond with the mushroom ketchup (or a splash of water if not using), scraping the browned bits up into the hash. Checkpoint — the sausage is browned and cooked through, the bacon rendered and glassy-edged, the black pudding crusted but intact — and every piece in the pan is now coated in the layered fond of all three. The hash smells like a full English already.
  3. **The vegetables — 6 minutes.** Add the onion and mushrooms, cook 3 minutes until the onion softens and the mushrooms brown, then the tomato dice for 2 minutes more, just to heat through and soften. Season with the remaining salt, pepper, and thyme, and taste the hash now — it should taste bold, a shade saltier than comfortable, because the eggs will mute it. Checkpoint — the hash is a uniformly browned, evenly seasoned mixture where every spoonful carries potato, meat, and vegetable in proportion; no pale onion, no raw-mushroom patches.
  4. **The wells and the eggs — 5 minutes, lidded.** Level the hash's surface, make 4 wells with the back of a spoon, drop the remaining 15 g butter around the hash's rim, and crack an egg into each well. Cover, reduce the heat to medium-low, and cook 4–5 minutes until the whites are just set and the yolks still tremble. Checkpoint — the whites are opaque from steam's gentle cook, the yolks dome liquid and wobble when the pan is nudged. The hash around them is still bubbling faintly at the edges. This is the dish finished — eggs baked into the breakfast itself.
  5. **Serve in the pan.** Bring the pan to the table on a board with the brown sauce alongside and toast cut into soldiers. Each serving is a wedge of hash with its egg — the yolk broken at the table and stirred through. Checkpoint — the eating test: the yolk runs into the hash's crevices, every forkful is potato-and-full-English together, and the pan's bottom layer (served last, fought over) is the crispest of all.

Finish & Plate

The pan itself is the presentation — a board, a trivet, four wedges cut with the edge of the spatula, each crowned with its egg. Toast soldiers for yolk-dipping, brown sauce for the hash, and the whole breakfast's washing-up is one pan and four forks.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Potatoes raw in the middleDice too large or steam stage skippedUniform 1.5 cm; the covered 10 minutes with water is what cooks them through
Hash turned to mashOver-stirred through the stagesTurn, don't stir; one deliberate fold per stage
Black pudding dissolved to crumbsAdded too early or diced too small1.5 cm dice, final 2 minutes of the meat stage only
Egg whites set, yolks hardHeat too high or lid left onMedium-low, and the straight-up lid check at 4 minutes
Hash tastes flatFond not scraped, seasoning shyDeglaze at stage 2's end; season bold before the eggs

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **Make-ahead:** the hash through stage 3 keeps 3 days refrigerated and reheats in the pan with a splash of water and 5 minutes — then the egg stage runs fresh on top. The hash also freezes 1 month; eggs always added on the day. - **Variation — bubble-and-squeak hash:** replace half the raw potato with 300 g cold cooked cabbage, squeezed and added with the vegetables; the dish becomes bubble-and-squeak with eggs in wells. - **Variation — the hot-smoked version:** 150 g hot-smoked salmon flaked in at the vegetable stage, eggs cracked over — a coastal café's deluxe, and the hash's most celebratory form. - **Scaling:** doubles to a roasting-tray version in a 200 °C oven — 30 minutes for the base, eggs in wells for the final 8 — the big-batch master's logic applied to hash.
